title: The road from Ta'if
hook: stoned out of Ta'if and bleeding, he is offered revenge, and refuses it
tomorrow: the Night Journey and the Hijra

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'am al-huzn, the year of sorrow. Your line was grief is a year, not a day.
screen: `GRIEF IS A YEAR, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: With his protector gone, Mecca is closing in, so the Prophet ﷺ walks up into the mountains to Ta'if, a cooler, greener town; later accounts say Zayd, the freed slave he raised as a son, walks with him. He asks its leaders: will you listen? Will you give me shelter? They don't just say no. They mock him. As he leaves, Ibn Ishaq says, they stir up the town's slaves and louts to shout after him. Later accounts add the stones: Zayd trying to shield him, and the Prophet's feet bleeding until his sandals were soaked.
screen: `A WALK TO TA'IF.` → `THEY MOCK HIM.` → `STONES, AND BLEEDING FEET.`

segments.voice: Years later, 'Aishah asked whether any day had been harder than the battle of Uhud. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his answer: the hardest was the day he went to a leader of Ta'if and was turned away. He walked on, dazed, not knowing where he was, until he looked up and saw a cloud shading him. In it was Jibril: Allah has heard what your people said to you. With him, the angel of the mountains: if you wish, I will bring the two mountains together and crush them. Bleeding, humiliated, with no one left to protect him, he's offered what a hurt person might want most: justice, revenge. The Prophet said no. Then this: I hope that Allah will bring out from their children people who will worship Allah alone. Not them. Their children. On the way home, Ibn Ishaq says, he rests in a garden, bleeding, and a servant named 'Addas brings him grapes. He says bismillah and eats. 'Addas is surprised: people here don't say that. Where are you from? Nineveh. And the Prophet answers: the town of the good man Yunus, son of Matta. He was my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet. Yunus, from day seventy-five. Turned away by a town himself, the Prophet calls a prophet from Nineveh his brother. The hope came true: years later, Ibn Ishaq says, Thaqif, the tribe of Ta'if, sent a delegation and accepted Islam. The Qur'an says to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.”
screen: `HARDER THAN UHUD.` · `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.` · `GRAPES, AND A MAN FROM NINEVEH.` · `THE HOPE CAME TRUE.` · then, large: `NOT THEM, THEIR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you, someone manageable, not the worst in your life; if part of you would like them to suffer a little, just notice it. Then, if you can, widen the frame to their children, the people who come after them. If you pray, you can ask Allah to guide them, or to bring good from what comes after them; if you don't, just wish their children well.
Ta'if, the town where he was stoned and offered revenge, and instead hoped for their children.
Your line: not them, their children. Tomorrow, a night journey, and the road out of Mecca. See you then.

screen: `DAY 94 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NIGHT JOURNEY AND THE HIJRA.`

howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ta'if as a picture of the Prophet's mercy toward those who hurt him, and it is recalled when Muslims are tempted to answer cruelty with revenge.

notes: Pickthall 21:107 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
Zayd accompanying him and the soaked sandals are from later seerah accounts (Ibn Sa'd and others); confirm.
The Bukhari hadith names the day as 'the day of 'Aqabah' and places the cloud at Qarn al-Tha'alib; most scholars link it to the Ta'if journey. Confirm.
'Within a generation' Thaqif accepted Islam (630–631, about a decade later). Confirm the phrasing.
